question: Which of the following is NOT correctly matched? [Count de Lally — Key sieges and military campaigns]
options: Fort St. David (Cuddalore) — Captured and completely demolished by Lally in 1758 shortly after his arrival in India
Battle of Wandiwash (1760) — Decisive battle where Lally was defeated by British General Sir Eyre Coote, ending French hopes in India
Pondicherry — The French capital which Lally defended during a long siege before surrendering to the British in 1761
Siege of Madras (1758–59) — Lally successfully captured Fort St. George, forcing the British presidency to surrender Madras
wrong_fact: Lally did NOT capture Madras; his Siege of Madras (1758-59) was a failure. Although he besieged Fort St. George for over two months, the arrival of a British naval squadron under Admiral Pocock forced him to lift the siege and retreat, which proved to be a major strategic turning point against the French.
explanation: Count de Lally (Thomas Arthur, Comte de Lally) arrived in India in 1758 as Governor-General of French India during the Third Carnatic War. He started with the successful capture and destruction of Fort St. David (Cuddalore). However, his subsequent Siege of Madras (1758–59) failed. In 1760, he was decisively defeated by Sir Eyre Coote at the Battle of Wandiwash, leading to the British siege and capture of Pondicherry in January 1761.

question: Which of the following is NOT correctly matched? [Count de Lally — Strategic retreats and political decisions]
options: Hyderabad (Deccan) — Lally recalled French General Bussy from the Nizam's court, weakening French influence in the Deccan
Tanjore (Thanjavur) — Lally led a failed campaign to extort money from the Maratha Raja of Tanjore, damaging French military prestige
Masulipatnam — Captured by the British under Colonel Forde in 1759 after French forces were weakened by Lally's recall of troops
Karikal — Lally successfully defended this French port on the Coromandel coast against all British naval and land attacks
wrong_fact: Karikal was NOT successfully defended by Lally. In April 1760, Karikal (a key French possession on the Coromandel coast) was attacked and captured by the British land forces under Major Monson and supported by the British navy, as the French fleet under Admiral D'Aché had abandoned the coast, leaving Karikal completely isolated.
explanation: Count de Lally's strategy was widely criticized. To concentrate forces in the Carnatic, he recalled Marquis de Bussy-Castelnau from Hyderabad, which destroyed French influence at the Nizam's court and allowed the British under Colonel Forde to capture Masulipatnam. Lally's siege of Tanjore (1758) failed to secure funds and exhausted his army. By 1760, French coastal outposts like Karikal fell to the British without effective French naval support.

question: Which of the following is NOT correctly matched? [Count de Lally — Fall of French factories and end of French rule]
options: Battle of Wandiwash (1760) — French forces were routed and Bussy was taken prisoner by the British
Fort St. David — Lally demolished the fortifications completely in 1758 to prevent the British from ever using it as a base again
Mahe (Malabar Coast) — Captured by the British in February 1761, representing the final capitulation of all French holdings in India
Chandernagore (Bengal) — Lally personally recaptured this Bengal factory from the British in 1759 using French reinforcements from Pondicherry
wrong_fact: Lally did NOT recapture Chandernagore. Chandernagore in Bengal had been captured by Robert Clive and Admiral Watson in March 1757, before Lally's arrival in India. The French never recaptured Chandernagore during the war; it remained under British control throughout Lally's campaign.
explanation: During the Third Carnatic War, the French lost all their Indian possessions. Chandernagore had already been captured by the British under Clive in 1757. Lally was unable to send any help to Bengal. In the south, the Battle of Wandiwash (1760) saw the defeat of the French and the capture of Bussy. Fort St. David was destroyed by Lally in 1758. Following the fall of Pondicherry in January 1761, the remaining French outpost at Mahe on the Malabar Coast surrendered in February 1761, completing the temporary total elimination of French power in India.
